stimuli.title: The Neighbor Who Knows the System
stimuli.text:
When Rosa Delgado's mother came home from the hospital, the family was handed a stack of papers: new medicines, three follow-up appointments and a diet sheet written in medical terms. Rosa remembers sitting at the kitchen table that night with no idea where to begin.

Help came from a woman named Joyce, a community health worker from the clinic down the street. Community health workers are not doctors or nurses. Most are trained members of the neighborhood they serve, and that is the point. Joyce spoke the family's language, knew which bus reached the specialist's office and understood why a patient might skip an appointment rather than lose a day's pay.

Over the next month, Joyce visited four times. She sorted the pills into a weekly box, helped Rosa call the pharmacy about a refill and translated the diet sheet into meals the family actually cooked. When Rosa's mother felt dizzy one afternoon, Joyce knew it was a reason to call the clinic, not wait.

Clinics that use health workers like Joyce report that patients keep more of their appointments and return to the hospital less often. The workers do not replace medical care. They connect people to it, filling the gap between a doctor's instructions and a family's daily life.

Rosa's mother is doing well now. Rosa, meanwhile, has signed up for the clinic's training course. "Someone showed us the way," she says. "I want to do that for the next family."

stimuli.title: From a story: The Last Bus
stimuli.text:
Darnell missed the 10:40 by about the length of a sneeze. He watched its taillights shrink down Fulton Avenue and felt the cold settle into his jacket like it planned to stay.

The next bus was not until 11:25. He had been on his feet since six that morning, stocking shelves, and his boss had asked him to stay late twice this week. Each time he had said yes, because saying no felt like stepping off a ledge.

A woman sat at the far end of the shelter, her grocery bags gathered around her ankles like sleeping cats. She glanced at him. "You work at the market on Grand," she said. "You found the soup I wanted last week. It was hiding behind the beans."

Darnell almost laughed. He had forgotten. To him it had been one question among a hundred, but she had carried it home with her.

They talked until the 11:25 came groaning around the corner. She was a night-school student, she said, studying to become a dental hygienist, and she was tired too. "Tired is just the price of the ticket," she told him. "You have to decide where the ticket goes."

On the ride home, Darnell took out his phone and looked at the community college page he had bookmarked months before. For the first time, he did not close it right away.

stimuli.title: Why Bread Rises
stimuli.text:
Bread dough is mostly flour and water, yet a loaf can double in size before it ever reaches the oven. The work is done by yeast, a living, single-celled fungus.

When yeast is mixed into dough, it feeds on sugars in the flour. As it breaks those sugars down, it releases carbon dioxide gas. On its own, the gas would simply escape. What traps it is gluten, a network of proteins that forms when flour is mixed with water and kneaded. Kneading stretches and lines up these proteins until the dough becomes elastic, able to hold thousands of tiny gas bubbles the way a balloon holds air.

Temperature controls the pace. Yeast is most active in a warm room; in a cold kitchen the dough rises slowly, and very hot water can kill the yeast before it starts. Many bakers let dough rise in a covered bowl so the surface does not dry out and crack.

In the oven, the heat makes the trapped gas expand one last time, a burst bakers call oven spring. Then the yeast dies, the gluten and starch firm up, and the bubbles are locked in place. Those bubbles are the holes you see when you slice the loaf.

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor: Light the Trail
stimuli.text:
To the editor:

The city council is deciding whether to add lights along the Riverside Trail, and I urge members to vote yes.

Hundreds of people use the trail to get to work, not just for exercise. In winter, it is dark by five o'clock, so anyone working a day shift walks or bikes home in the dark. I have spoken with nurses from the hospital and cooks from the restaurants on Main Street who now take a longer route along busy roads because they do not feel safe on the trail at night.

Lighting would also bring the trail more use. When the neighboring town of Millbrook lit its river path, its parks department counted about forty percent more evening users the next year. More people on a path means more eyes on it, which makes it safer for everyone.

Some council members worry about the cost. But the plan uses solar-powered lamps, which need no wiring and have low running costs. My own electric bill has gone up every year since I moved here, which shows how much energy costs are rising.

Our trail is one of the best things about this city. Let's make sure people can use it all year, not only in summer.

Alicia Grant, Elm Street

stimuli.title: Report: First Year of the Downtown Bike Share
stimuli.text:
The downtown bike share opened last April with 60 bikes at 8 stations. The program's goal was to give residents a cheap way to make short trips and to reduce traffic in the business district. This report covers the first twelve months.

Riders took trips in every month of the year, though use dropped sharply in winter. The busiest station was beside the train depot, where many commuters ride the last mile to their offices. The quietest was at the east end of the park, which planners now think was placed too far from the shops and homes riders come from.

| Season | Trips taken | Average trip length |
|---|---|---|
| Spring | 4,100 | 14 minutes |
| Summer | 6,300 | 18 minutes |
| Fall | 3,900 | 13 minutes |
| Winter | 1,200 | 9 minutes |

Two changes are planned for the second year. The east park station will move two blocks closer to the shopping street, and 20 bikes will be added at the depot, where riders often found the racks empty during the morning rush.

stimuli.title: Gardens on Empty Lots
stimuli.text:
Ten years ago, the lot at the corner of Pine and Third was a patch of broken glass and weeds. Today it holds thirty raised beds, a tool shed and a bench where older neighbors sit in the shade of a young maple.

The change began when a group of residents asked the city whether they could clean up the lot. The city owned it but had no plans for it, so it agreed to a one-year lease for one dollar. Volunteers hauled away trash, trucked in clean soil and built the beds from donated lumber. Because the old soil might contain lead from paint and car exhaust, they grew food only in the new raised beds, never in the ground.

Each bed is assigned to a household for the season. Some families grow tomatoes and peppers; others grow herbs used in dishes from home. A shared bed at the front supplies a nearby food pantry with fresh vegetables every week from June to October.

The garden has grown more than food. Neighbors who had lived on the same block for years without speaking now trade seeds and recipes. A retired electrician teaches teenagers to build compost bins. When a storm knocked the shed's roof loose last spring, it was repaired by noon.

The city has since renewed the lease for five years and has opened two more empty lots to gardeners.

stimuli.title: From a story: Inventory
stimuli.text:
On her first morning at the warehouse, Mei was handed a scanner gun, an orange vest and a map of aisles that looked like a maze drawn by someone who disliked mazes.

"Pick list comes up on the screen," said Carl, the shift lead, without looking up from his clipboard. "Scan the shelf, scan the box, put it in the cart. Don't skip the shelf scan." Then he was gone.

By ten o'clock Mei had walked what felt like the length of the state. She had also skipped the shelf scan twice, to save time, and both times the gun had buzzed at her like an angry wasp. The second time, a box of phone chargers she had grabbed turned out to be the wrong model.

At lunch, an older picker named Ruthie slid into the seat across from her. "Carl tell you not to skip the shelf scan?" Mei nodded, cheeks hot. "He told me the same thing nine years ago," Ruthie said. "I skipped it for a week. Then I sent a hospital a carton of the wrong gloves." She unwrapped her sandwich. "Slow hands, fast feet. That's the whole job."

In the afternoon Mei scanned every shelf. Her cart filled more slowly at first, and then, somehow, faster. When the shift ended, Carl glanced at her numbers and raised one eyebrow, which she would later learn was his highest form of praise.

stimuli.title: How a Heat Pump Moves Heat
stimuli.text:
A furnace makes heat by burning fuel or by running electricity through a heating element. A heat pump works differently: it does not make heat so much as move it from one place to another.

The key is a fluid called a refrigerant, which boils at a very low temperature. In heating mode, the refrigerant flows through coils in an outdoor unit. Even on a cold day, the outdoor air holds some heat, and that heat is enough to make the cold refrigerant boil into a gas. A compressor then squeezes the gas, which raises its temperature sharply. The hot gas flows to a coil inside the house, where a fan blows air across it. The refrigerant gives up its heat to the indoor air, cools and turns back into a liquid, and the cycle starts again.

In summer, a valve reverses the flow. The indoor coil now absorbs heat from the house, and the outdoor unit releases it outside, so the same machine works as an air conditioner.

Because moving heat takes less energy than making it, a heat pump can deliver more heat energy than the electrical energy it uses. Its advantage shrinks in very cold weather, when there is less heat in the outdoor air to collect, so homes in the coldest climates often keep a backup heat source.

stimuli.title: Two Views: Phones at Work
stimuli.text:
**Text A: from a company newsletter**

Starting next month, personal phones must stay in lockers during shifts on the production floor. Last year we had six incidents in which a worker looking at a phone stepped into the path of a forklift. Two people were hurt. Phones may be used freely in the break room and during lunch, and the floor supervisor's line will be posted so families can reach workers in an emergency. Safety on the floor comes first.

**Text B: from a letter by a production worker**

I understand the concern about forklifts, but a total ban goes too far. Most of the incidents happened in one loading area where the walkways are not marked, and painting clear lanes there would fix the real problem. Many of us are parents. When a school calls, waiting for a message to pass through a supervisor could take an hour. A better rule would let workers carry phones but use them only in marked safe areas. Treat us as adults who can follow a reasonable rule.

stimuli.title: Notice: Free Flu Shots at the Library
stimuli.text:
The county health department will give free flu shots at three library branches this fall. No appointment is needed, and no insurance is required. Adults and children 6 months and older may get a shot. Children under 18 must come with a parent or guardian.

Please bring a photo ID if you have one. If you have had a serious reaction to a flu shot in the past, talk with your doctor before you come. Wear a short-sleeved shirt or one with sleeves that roll up easily.

| Branch | Date | Hours |
|---|---|---|
| Central Library | Saturday, October 3 | 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. |
| Eastside Branch | Tuesday, October 6 | 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. |
| Hillcrest Branch | Thursday, October 8 | 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. |

Each clinic will close early if the vaccine runs out, so plan to arrive well before closing time. Shots take about ten minutes, plus a short wait afterward so staff can make sure you feel well.

stimuli.title: Sleep and Memory
stimuli.text:
Many people treat sleep as wasted time, the hours they could be working or studying if only they did not need them. Brain researchers see it very differently. Sleep, it turns out, is when much of the day's learning gets saved.

During the day, new information is held for a short time in a part of the brain called the hippocampus. During deep sleep, the brain replays some of that activity and moves important patterns into longer-term storage. In studies, people who learned a list of words and then slept remembered more of them the next day than people who learned the same list and stayed awake for the same number of hours.

Sleep also seems to help with skills, not only facts. People practicing a new finger-tapping sequence were often faster and more accurate after a night's sleep, even though they had not practiced again.

The lesson for students is a practical one. Staying up all night to cram can leave a person with less, not more, to show for the effort. Studying in shorter sessions over several days, with real sleep in between, gives the brain more chances to do its overnight work.

stimuli.title: From a story: The Letter
stimuli.text:
The envelope sat on the kitchen counter for three days. Andre walked past it on his way to work, on his way back, on his way to bed. It had the community college's seal in the corner, a small blue lamp, and it was thin. Thin envelopes, everyone said, meant no.

His daughter, Kiana, noticed on the second day. "You're not going to open it?" she asked.

"I'll get to it," he said, in the voice he used for the electric bill.

On the third night, Kiana sat across from him at the table, her chin in her hands, and simply waited. She was eleven and had recently discovered that silence could be a kind of argument.

Andre sighed and slit the envelope with a butter knife. He read the single page once, then again, his lips moving slightly, as they did when he read anything that mattered.

"Well?" Kiana said.

He set the page down and smoothed it flat with both hands, the way his own father used to smooth a map. "Classes start in January," he said. His voice came out smaller than he meant it to. Kiana was already out of her chair, and for once he did not tell her to stop shouting.

stimuli.title: Opinion: Give Buses Their Own Lane
stimuli.text:
Every weekday morning, the Number 9 bus carries more people down Grand Avenue than all the cars on that street put together, and it moves slower than any of them. The bus is stuck in the same traffic, stopping every few blocks to let riders on and off. The city should paint a lane on Grand for buses only.

Bus lanes work because a bus full of riders takes up far less road space per person than cars do. When a bus no longer waits behind traffic, trips get faster, and faster trips bring more riders.

The city's own trial last spring showed what is possible. For six weeks, one lane on Grand was closed to cars during the morning rush.

| Morning trip on Grand Avenue | Before the trial | During the trial |
|---|---|---|
| Average bus trip time | 31 minutes | 22 minutes |
| Average car trip time | 18 minutes | 19 minutes |
| Average weekday bus riders | 2,400 | 2,900 |

Shop owners worried that fewer parking spaces would mean fewer customers. But most people who shop on Grand arrive on foot or by bus, and a faster bus brings more of them. Besides, the avenue's new murals have made it one of the most photographed streets in the city.

The trial is over, and the lane is gone. It is time to bring it back for good.

stimuli.title: Two Accounts of the River Street Flood
stimuli.text:
**Account 1: from the local newspaper**

Heavy rain on Tuesday night pushed Mill Creek over its banks, flooding the lower end of River Street with up to two feet of water. Fire crews evacuated eleven homes by boat. No injuries were reported. City officials said the storm drains were working but could not keep up with nearly four inches of rain in three hours. Cleanup began Wednesday, and the street reopened to traffic Thursday morning.

**Account 2: from a resident's blog**

By ten o'clock Tuesday the water was at our front step, and by midnight it was in the living room. We had reported the clogged drain at the corner twice this year and nothing was done, so I do not believe it was working that night. Our neighbors were wonderful. The Okafors took in our dog, and a teenager from down the block helped us carry the photo albums upstairs. We are still pulling up wet carpet.

stimuli.title: Draft: A proposal for recycling bins
stimuli.text: (1) Our warehouse throws away a huge amount of cardboard every week. (2) Most of it goes straight into the trash compactor, even though nearly all of it could be recycled. (3) I think we should put recycling bins beside each packing station. (4) Last month I counted the boxes we broke down on my shift, and there were more than three hundred. (5) The recycling company that serves our area picks up cardboard for businesses at no charge. (6) My cousin works at a recycling plant in another state. (7) Fewer trash pickups could also lower what the company pays to haul away waste. (8) Bins would take up very little floor space.

stimuli.title: Draft: How to jump-start a car
stimuli.text: (1) A dead battery does not have to ruin your day if you have jumper cables and a second car. (2) First, park the working car close to the dead one and turn both engines off. (3) Clip one red clamp to the positive post of the dead battery. (4) Clip the other red clamp to the positive post of the good battery. (5) Next, attach a black clamp to the negative post of the good battery. (6) Attach the last black clamp to a bare metal part of the dead car's engine, away from the battery. (7) Start the working car and let it run for a few minutes before trying the other.

stimuli.title: Draft: Letter about pool hours
stimuli.text: (1) Dear Parks Director: (2) I am writing to ask that the Lincoln Street pool stay open until 8 p.m. on summer weeknights. (3) Right now the pool closes at 6 p.m., before many parents get home from work. (4) Families who work during the day have no chance to swim together. (5) On hot evenings, children in our neighborhood end up playing in the street to cool off. (6) The pool on Cedar Avenue has a great snack bar. (7) Two extra hours, five nights a week, would let many more residents use a pool their taxes already pay for. (8) Thank you for considering this request.

stimuli.title: Draft: The town's first library
stimuli.text: (1) Our town's first public library opened in 1912 in a single room above the hardware store. (2) It held about four hundred books, most of them donated by local families. (3) The library grew quickly. (4) By 1930, it had moved into its own brick building on Main Street. (5) The building was paid for by a fundraising drive in which schoolchildren collected pennies door to door. (6) Today that building is the town museum, and the library has moved again, to a larger space beside the high school.

stimuli.title: Draft: Why our clinic should offer evening hours
stimuli.text: (1) The Westside Health Clinic is open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. (2) For people who work those same hours, getting a checkup means losing a day's pay. (3) The clinic should stay open until 7 p.m. two nights a week. (4) A survey of clinic patients found that more than half work daytime shifts. (5) Many of them said they skip checkups because they cannot leave work. (6) Evening hours would help patients get care before small problems become serious. (7) The clinic's waiting room was painted last year.

stimuli.title: Draft: How to plant a tree
stimuli.text: (1) Planting a tree correctly helps it live for decades. (2) Dig a hole two to three times as wide as the root ball but no deeper than it. (3) Remove the container and gently loosen any roots that circle the ball. (4) Set the tree in the hole so the top of the root ball is level with the ground. (5) Fill the hole with the soil you removed, pressing lightly to remove air pockets. (6) Water the tree deeply, and spread mulch around it, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the trunk.

stimuli.title: Draft: Report on honeybees
stimuli.text: (1) Honeybees live in colonies that can hold tens of thousands of bees. (2) Each colony has one queen, whose main job is to lay eggs. (3) Most of the other bees are female workers. (4) Workers do almost every job in the hive: they clean, build wax comb, guard the entrance and gather nectar and pollen. (5) A few hundred male bees, called drones, also live in the hive. (6) Their only job is to mate with a queen from another colony.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Health workers connect people to care
Hospital paperwork is too hard to read
Clinics need more doctors and nurses
Rosa wants to train as a nurse someday
questions.explanation: The passage shows Joyce helping one family follow its care plan and then says such workers "connect people" to medical care. Rosa's training is one detail near the end, and she is training as a health worker, not a nurse.

questions.stem: Why was Joyce able to help the family in ways a doctor might not?
options: She knew the neighborhood's daily life
She had trained at the same hospital
She worked longer hours than the doctors
questions.explanation: The passage says health workers are usually members of the neighborhood they serve: Joyce spoke the family's language and knew the bus routes and the pressures of lost pay. She is not a doctor, so she could not prescribe medicine.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that health workers improve patients' care?
options: Joyce visited the family four times
Rosa sat at the kitchen table that night
Patients keep more of their appointments
The clinic is down the street
questions.explanation: Keeping appointments and fewer hospital returns are results that show better care. Four visits shows Joyce's effort, not an outcome.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, what does "filling the gap" mean?
questions.explanation: The gap is the space between a doctor's instructions and a family's daily life, and the workers cover what is missing there. The sentence before says they do not replace medical care, so taking someone's job is wrong.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the passage with Rosa's quotation?
options: To show the help being passed on
To explain how the course works
To argue that clinics should pay more
questions.explanation: Rosa says someone showed her family the way and she wants to do the same for the next family, so the ending shows the help continuing. The quotation says nothing about how the course works.

questions.stem: Which theme does the story develop?
options: A small moment can change a life
Working hard always leads to success
questions.explanation: A short talk with a stranger leads Darnell to look at the college page and, for once, not close it. The story shows two tired workers; it never claims hard work always pays off.

questions.stem: Why had Darnell agreed to stay late at work twice that week?
options: He needed the extra pay for school
Refusing felt too risky to him
His boss promised him a promotion
questions.explanation: The story says saying no "felt like stepping off a ledge": refusing seemed dangerous to him. Nothing in the story mentions pay for school or a promotion.

questions.stem: What does the simile "like sleeping cats" suggest about the woman's grocery bags?
options: They were full of pet food
They kept sliding around the floor
They sat in a quiet, cozy heap
questions.explanation: Sleeping cats curl up close and still, so the bags sit gathered and quiet at her feet. The simile describes how they look, not what is in them.

questions.stem: What does the woman mean when she says, "Tired is just the price of the ticket"?
options: Tiredness is the cost of a goal
People should rest before they travel
questions.explanation: The ticket stands for a path toward something, and being tired is what it costs. She then says you have to decide where the ticket goes, which is about choosing a goal, not about fares.

questions.stem: How does the third-person narration shape the story?
options: It shows every rider's thoughts equally
It lets the woman tell her own story
questions.explanation: The narrator tells us what Darnell feels and remembers, such as forgetting the soup, but the woman is known only by what she says. The narration reveals Darnell's feelings rather than hiding them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what keeps the gas from escaping the dough?
options: The cover on the rising bowl
questions.explanation: The passage says the gas would escape on its own and that gluten traps it, like a balloon holding air. The covered bowl only keeps the surface from drying out.

questions.stem: What happens right after the trapped gas expands in the oven?
options: The baker kneads the dough once again
The yeast starts feeding on sugar
The yeast dies and the loaf firms up
questions.explanation: The last paragraph gives the order: oven spring, then the yeast dies and the gluten and starch firm up. Feeding on sugar happens much earlier, in the dough.

questions.stem: As it is used in the passage, what does "elastic" mean?
questions.explanation: The passage says kneading makes the dough elastic, "able to hold" gas bubbles like a balloon, so it stretches without tearing. Warmth affects yeast, not elasticity.

questions.stem: How is most of the passage organized?
options: As a comparison of two breads
As a problem and its solution
questions.explanation: The passage follows bread from mixing to rising to baking, explaining each stage in order. It never compares two breads.

questions.stem: What does the writer want the city council to do?
options: Build a new route on Main Street
questions.explanation: The letter opens by urging members to vote yes on lights for the Riverside Trail and ends by asking that people can use it all year.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention nurses and cooks?
options: To show that workers dislike the trail
To describe jobs on Main Street
To prove the hospital supports the plan
To show people ride it to their jobs
questions.explanation: The writer says the trail is used to get to work, then gives nurses and cooks as examples of day-shift workers who now avoid it after dark. The writer never says the hospital backs the plan.

questions.stem: Which sentence does not support the writer's argument?
options: My own electric bill has gone up every year
More people on a path means more eyes on it
It is dark by five o'clock in winter
questions.explanation: The writer's home electric bill says nothing about the cost of solar trail lamps, which need no wiring. The other sentences support the need for lights or their benefit.

questions.stem: What would make the Millbrook evidence stronger?
options: A photo of the Millbrook path
Safety data from after the lights
A list of other trails in the state
questions.explanation: The writer claims lights make the trail safer, but the Millbrook figure counts users only. Safety data after lighting would test that claim directly.

questions.stem: Why will the east park station be moved?
options: It had more bikes than it needed
It was far from riders' homes
questions.explanation: The report says planners think the station was placed too far from the shops and homes riders come from. The busiest station was the one beside the depot.

questions.stem: Why are bikes being added at the depot?
options: The depot station was the quietest
Racks there ran out at rush hour
questions.explanation: The report says riders often found the depot racks empty during the morning rush, which means demand there was higher than the supply.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, what does "the last mile" most likely mean?
options: The short last part of a trip
A race at the end of the year
The very end of the bike path
questions.explanation: Commuters arrive by train and ride the rest of the way to their offices, so the last mile is the short final stretch of the trip.

questions.stem: What do the table and the text together show about winter?
options: The program closed for the season
Most trips started at the park
Trips were longer than in fall
questions.explanation: The text says use dropped sharply in winter, and the table shows the fewest trips (1,200) and the shortest average (9 minutes). Riders took trips in every month, so it did not close.

questions.stem: At 6 a.m. the temperature was $-8$ degrees Fahrenheit. By noon it had risen 15 degrees. What was the temperature at noon?
questions.explanation: Rising 15 degrees from $-8$ means $-8 + 15 = 7$. Getting 23 comes from adding 8 and 15 as if both were positive.

questions.stem: Which list orders the numbers from least to greatest?
questions.explanation: Among negatives, the one farther from zero is smaller, so $-3 < -2.5$. Then $0.4 < 0.5$, and $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$. Putting $-2.5$ first treats it as smaller because 2.5 is less than 3.

questions.stem: A 12-ounce bottle of shampoo costs \$3.60. What is the price per ounce?
questions.explanation: Unit price is total cost divided by ounces: $3.60 \div 12 = 0.30$, or 30 cents an ounce. \$0.36 comes from dividing by 10 instead of 12.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of milk. How many cups of flour go with 8 cups of milk?
questions.explanation: 8 cups of milk is 4 times 2 cups, so the flour is 4 times 3 cups: 12 cups. Adding instead of multiplying (8 + 1) gives 9.

questions.stem: Maria worked $\frac{3}{4}$ of an hour on Monday and $1\frac{1}{2}$ hours on Tuesday. How many hours did she work in all?
questions.explanation: Write $1\frac{1}{2}$ as $1\frac{2}{4}$; then $\frac{3}{4} + 1\frac{2}{4} = 1\frac{5}{4} = 2\frac{1}{4}$. Adding tops and bottoms separately gives the wrong $1\frac{4}{6}$.

questions.stem: Between which two whole numbers is $\sqrt{50}$?
questions.explanation: $7^2 = 49$ and $8^2 = 64$, and 50 is between them, so $\sqrt{50}$ is a little more than 7. 24 and 25 come from halving 50 instead of taking its root.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $3x - 7 = 20$ true?
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides to get $3x = 27$, then divide by 3: $x = 9$. Subtracting 7 instead gives $3x = 13$, which is not a whole number.

questions.stem: A plumber charges a \$45 visit fee plus \$30 for each hour of work. Which expression gives the total charge, in dollars, for $h$ hours?
questions.explanation: The \$45 fee is paid once and the \$30 is paid for each hour, so the total is $45 + 30h$. $75h$ wrongly charges the fee every hour.

questions.stem: Which shows 0.00052 in scientific notation?
questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 5.2, so the power is $10^{-4}$. A positive exponent would make a large number, 52,000.

questions.stem:
The cost $y$, in dollars, of renting a kayak for $x$ hours is shown.

| Hours $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost $y$ | 18 | 26 | 34 |

Which equation fits the table?
questions.explanation: The cost rises 8 for each hour, so the slope is 8; at $x = 1$, $8 + 10 = 18$, so the start value is 10. $y = 8x + 18$ gives 26 for one hour, not 18.

questions.stem: Which value of $x$ makes $2x + 5 > 17$ true?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5 and divide by 2: $x > 6$. Only 7 is greater than 6; $x = 6$ gives exactly 17, which is not greater than 17.

questions.stem: A student's five quiz scores are 82, 90, 75, 90 and 88. What is the mean score?
questions.explanation: The total is $82 + 90 + 75 + 90 + 88 = 425$, and $425 \div 5 = 85$. The mode, 90, is the most common score, not the mean.

questions.stem: On one street, four homes sold for about \$200,000 each and one sold for \$1,000,000. Which measure best describes a typical price on the street?
questions.explanation: One very high price pulls the mean far above what most homes sold for, but the median stays at the middle value, about \$200,000.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red, 6 blue and 10 green marbles. One marble is drawn without looking. What is the probability it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 6 blue marbles out of $4 + 6 + 10 = 20$, and $\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$. $\frac{3}{5}$ compares blue with green only.

questions.stem: A city wants to know how all residents feel about a new park. Which sample is most likely to represent them?
options: The first 200 people to reply online
questions.explanation: A random sample gives every resident the same chance to be picked. Park visitors and hikers are more likely to favor parks than residents as a whole.

questions.stem:
A company surveyed 100 workers about how they get to work.

| Shift | Drive | Take the bus |
|---|---|---|
| Day | 40 | 20 |
| Night | 30 | 10 |

What percent of night-shift workers take the bus?
questions.explanation: There are $30 + 10 = 40$ night-shift workers, and 10 of them take the bus: $\frac{10}{40} = 25\%$. 10% divides by all 100 workers instead of the night shift.

questions.stem: On a floor plan, 1 inch stands for 4 feet. A room is 3.5 inches long on the plan. How long is the real room?
questions.explanation: Each inch is 4 feet, so $3.5 \times 4 = 14$ feet. Adding 4 to 3.5 gives 7.5, which mixes up multiplying and adding.

questions.stem: A round rug has a radius of 3 feet. Using 3.14 for $\pi$, what is its area?
questions.explanation: $A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times 3^2 = 3.14 \times 9 = 28.26$ square feet. 18.84 is the circumference, $2\pi r$.

questions.stem: Two angles are supplementary. One measures 65 degrees. How many degrees does the other measure?
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees: $180 - 65 = 115$. Using 90, the total for complementary angles, gives 25.

questions.stem: A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
questions.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse: $5^2 + h^2 = 13^2$, so $h^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$ and $h = 12$. Subtracting the lengths, $13 - 5$, gives 8.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the writer's main claim?
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 says what the writer wants: recycling bins beside each packing station. Sentence 1 describes the problem that leads to the claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it does not support the claim?
questions.explanation: Where the writer's cousin works gives no reason to add bins at this warehouse. Sentence 5, free pickup, is one of the strongest reasons.

questions.stem: Which detail would best strengthen sentence 4?
options: How long the writer has worked there
A weekly box count for all shifts
The name of the packing station lead
questions.explanation: Sentence 4 counts boxes on one shift; a count for the whole warehouse would show the full size of the problem.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best conclude the proposal?
options: I will be on vacation next week.
Bins would cut costs and waste.
questions.explanation: A conclusion should sum up the claim and its main reasons: savings and recycling. The other sentences add unrelated facts.

questions.stem: Which word or phrase would best begin sentence 3?
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 is the next step after parking and turning the engines off, so a sequence word fits. However and In contrast signal opposing ideas.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 7 to finish the steps?
options: My uncle taught me this when I was a teenager.
Last, start the dead car and remove the cables.
Batteries come in many different sizes and shapes.
Always carry a spare tire in your trunk too.
questions.explanation: The steps stop before the dead car is started and the cables removed, so the missing final step completes the process. The other sentences are off topic.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of sentence 1?
options: To list the tools in order
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 tells the reader what the passage is about and when they would need it; the steps start with sentence 2.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Each of the drivers ___ a safety vest."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The subject is each, which is singular, so the verb is wears. Drivers is in a prepositional phrase and does not control the verb.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The manager asked Luis and ___ to stay late."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is an object of asked, so it is me. Test it alone: "asked me," not "asked I."

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The bus was late, we missed the start of the meeting."

Which revision is correct?
questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma are a comma splice. Adding the conjunction so after the comma fixes it.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"All of the ___ lockers were cleaned on Friday."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The lockers belong to many workers, so the plural possessive takes the apostrophe after the s. Worker's means one worker.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
options: We drove to ohio last Thanksgiving.
We Drove to Ohio last Thanksgiving.
We drove to Ohio last thanksgiving.
We drove to Ohio last Thanksgiving.
questions.explanation: States and holidays are proper nouns, so Ohio and Thanksgiving are capitalized; drove is an ordinary verb.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"At this point in time, the store is currently hiring new employees."

Which revision is the most concise?
options: The store is hiring new employees.
At this time, the store is currently hiring.
Currently the store hires new employees now.
The store, at this point, is hiring employees now.
questions.explanation: "At this point in time" and "currently" repeat the same idea, so dropping both keeps the meaning in the fewest words: The store is hiring new employees. The other choices still repeat the idea of now or drop part of the meaning.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The new rule is mandatory, so every worker must follow it."

What does mandatory mean?
questions.explanation: The clue is "every worker must follow it," so mandatory means required. Optional is the opposite.

questions.stem: The root port means "carry." Which word means "able to be carried"?
questions.explanation: The suffix -able means "able to be," so portable means able to be carried. Transport means to carry from one place to another, not able to be carried.

questions.stem:
Read the sentences.

"The job pays well. ___, the commute is very long."

Which word best fills the blank?
questions.explanation: A long commute is a drawback that contrasts with good pay, so a contrast word fits. Therefore would mean the long commute is caused by the pay.

questions.stem: A worker is writing a report for a supervisor. Which sentence fits a formal report best?
options: The shipment arrived two days late.
The boxes were, like, really late.
The shipment showed up super late, ugh.
So yeah, the stuff came late.
questions.explanation: A report uses clear, neutral wording. Slang such as super, ugh and like is too casual for a supervisor.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The nurse will chart the patient's temperature every hour."

What does chart mean in this sentence?
questions.explanation: Here chart is a verb meaning to write down information in a patient's record. A chart can also be a map, but here the nurse is writing down a reading.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: The city sold its empty lots
Lead in the soil makes gardens unsafe
questions.explanation: The passage traces the lot's change into a garden and stresses that it "has grown more than food": neighbors now know and help one another. Lead is one detail about why beds are raised.

questions.stem: Why did the volunteers grow food only in raised beds?
options: The city did not allow digging
The old soil might have lead
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the old soil might contain lead from paint and car exhaust, so food went only in beds of new soil.

questions.stem: How does the shed repair connect to the rest of the passage?
options: It shows neighbors now pitch in as a team
It proves the shed was poorly built
It shows that storms damage gardens
It explains why the lease was renewed
questions.explanation: The repair comes in the paragraph about neighbors trading seeds and teaching teenagers, and its quick fix by noon shows their new teamwork. The passage never links the repair to the lease.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin with the lot as it was ten years ago?
options: To show that weeds grow fast
To contrast it with the garden today
To blame the city for the trash
To explain how the soil got polluted
questions.explanation: Broken glass and weeds are set against the thirty beds, shed and bench of today, so the opening sets up a before-and-after contrast.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, what does "renewed" mean?
questions.explanation: The first lease was for one year; the city has since renewed it for five years, so it was extended. A cancelled lease would not let gardening continue.

questions.stem: How does Mei change during the day?
options: She decides to quit the job
She becomes the new shift lead
questions.explanation: In the morning Mei skips the shelf scan to save time and makes a mistake; after Ruthie's story she scans every shelf. She does not quit, and Carl is still the shift lead.

questions.stem: Which lesson does Ruthie's story teach Mei?
options: Careful work ends up saving time
New workers make the most mistakes
questions.explanation: Ruthie's mistake with the gloves and her motto "Slow hands, fast feet" show that care prevents costly errors; by afternoon Mei's cart fills faster.

questions.stem: What does the comparison of the scanner to "an angry wasp" show?
options: The warning was sharp and annoying
Mei was terribly afraid of insects
The warehouse had a pest problem
questions.explanation: A wasp's buzz is sharp and unwelcome, so the comparison shows how the warning sounded to Mei. The scanner was working: it caught her skipped scans.

questions.stem: What does the description of the map as "a maze drawn by someone who disliked mazes" add to the story?
options: A clue that Carl drew the map
A warning that the warehouse is unsafe
A note of humor about Mei's confusion
A hint that Mei is good with maps
questions.explanation: The exaggeration is playful: it makes the reader smile at how lost Mei feels on her first morning. Nothing suggests Carl drew it.

questions.stem: What does the last sentence suggest about Carl?
options: He did not notice Mei at all
He is unhappy with Mei's work
questions.explanation: Raising one eyebrow is called his highest form of praise, so he approves of her numbers but shows it in a small way. That also rules out frequent praise.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how is a heat pump different from a furnace?
options: It moves heat instead of making it
It burns its fuel more slowly
It works only in the summer months
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says a furnace makes heat while a heat pump moves it from one place to another. The passage says it uses electrical energy, so it does need electricity.

questions.stem: Why do homes in the coldest places often keep a backup heat source?
options: The compressor works only in summer
Cold air holds less heat to collect
The valve cannot reverse in winter
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the heat pump's advantage shrinks in very cold weather, when there is less heat in the outdoor air. Nothing says the refrigerant freezes.

questions.stem: As it is used in the passage, what is a "refrigerant"?
options: A valve that reverses the flow in summer
A fan that blows warm air indoors
A fluid with a very low boiling point
A coil inside the outdoor unit
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines it: "a fluid called a refrigerant, which boils at a very low temperature." The fan, valve and coils are separate parts.

questions.stem: What does the third paragraph add to the explanation?
options: Why heat pumps cost less to install
How the machine also cools a house
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that a valve reverses the flow so the machine works as an air conditioner in summer.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes Text B?
options: Mark lanes and allow phones in safe areas
Workers should ignore the new rule
Ban phones from the whole building
Forklifts should be removed from the floor
questions.explanation: The worker argues for marking lanes in the loading area and letting workers carry phones but use them only in marked safe areas. The letter asks for a better rule, not for workers to ignore it.

questions.stem: How does the worker in Text B respond to the safety concern in Text A?
options: Agrees that a total ban is needed
Agrees it is real but blames another cause
Says the incidents never actually happened
questions.explanation: Text B opens "I understand the concern about forklifts" and then says unmarked walkways in one area caused most incidents. It accepts the problem but disputes the cause.

questions.stem: On which point do the two texts disagree?
options: Whether forklifts operate on the floor
How families can reach workers in time
Whether phones are allowed at lunch
questions.explanation: Text A says the supervisor's line lets families reach workers in an emergency; Text B says a message through a supervisor could take an hour. Neither text disputes lunch use or the injuries.

questions.stem: Which fact would most strengthen the argument in Text B?
options: Phones are already allowed in the break room
Most incidents were in the unmarked area
questions.explanation: Text B's main claim is that the real problem is the unmarked walkways, so proof that the incidents cluster there supports a fix other than a ban. Being a parent supports the need for phones, not the safety claim.

questions.stem: Who must come with a parent or guardian?
questions.explanation: The notice says children under 18 must come with a parent or guardian. Children under 6 months cannot get the shot at all.

questions.stem: Why does the notice advise arriving well before closing time?
options: The vaccine may run out early
Shots take an hour to give
The line is longest at the end
questions.explanation: The notice says each clinic will close early if the vaccine runs out. Shots take about ten minutes, not an hour.

questions.stem: Why does the notice mention short sleeves?
options: To keep people cool while waiting
So the arm can be reached quickly
Because long sleeves are not allowed
questions.explanation: The shot is given in the upper arm, so sleeves that roll up easily save time. The notice suggests a choice of shirts, not a rule.

questions.stem: A parent works until 4 p.m. on weekdays. Which clinic fits best?
questions.explanation: The table shows Eastside open 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. on a Tuesday, after the parent's workday. Hillcrest closes at 2 p.m., and the Central Library clinic is on Saturday.

questions.stem: A diver is 30 feet below the surface, at $-30$ feet. She rises 12 feet. What is her new position?
questions.explanation: Rising adds: $-30 + 12 = -18$ feet, still below the surface. $-42$ comes from moving 12 feet deeper instead.

questions.stem: A jacket that costs \$80 is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: 25% of 80 is $0.25 \times 80 = 20$, and $80 - 20 = 60$. \$20 is the discount, not the price.

questions.stem: A walker covers $\frac{1}{2}$ mile in $\frac{1}{4}$ hour. At this rate, how many miles does she walk in one hour?
questions.explanation: Divide distance by time: $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 = 2$ miles per hour. Multiplying the fractions gives $\frac{1}{8}$.

questions.stem: On a coordinate grid, point $P$ is at $(-3, 4)$ and point $Q$ is at $(5, 4)$. How far apart are the points?
questions.explanation: The points share $y = 4$, so the distance is the gap in $x$: $|5 - (-3)| = 8$. Getting 2 comes from $5 - 3$, ignoring the negative sign.

questions.stem: A $7\frac{1}{2}$-pound bag of rice is split into smaller bags of $\frac{3}{4}$ pound each. How many smaller bags are filled?
questions.explanation: $7\frac{1}{2} = \frac{15}{2}$, and $\frac{15}{2} \div \frac{3}{4} = \frac{15}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} = 10$. Multiplying instead of dividing gives about $5\frac{5}{8}$.

questions.stem: Which set of pairs $(x, y)$ shows a proportional relationship?
questions.explanation: In a proportional relationship $y \div x$ is the same for every pair; here it is always 3. In (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 8) the ratio changes, because the pattern starts at 2, not 0.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $4(x - 3) = 28$ true?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 4 to get $x - 3 = 7$, then add 3: $x = 10$. Forgetting to multiply the 3 by 4 when expanding leads to a wrong value of 7.75.

questions.stem: Which is equal to $2^3 \cdot 2^4$?
questions.explanation: When powers of the same base are multiplied, add the exponents: $2^{3+4} = 2^7$. Multiplying the exponents gives $2^{12}$, which is far too large.

questions.stem: Two numbers add up to 20, and one is 6 more than the other. What are the numbers?
questions.explanation: If the smaller is $n$, then $n + (n + 6) = 20$, so $2n = 14$ and $n = 7$; the other is 13. 14 and 6 add to 20 but differ by 8.

questions.skill: Initial value of a linear model
questions.stem: The cost $C$, in dollars, of a gym membership for $m$ months is $C = 25m + 40$. What does the 40 stand for?
questions.explanation: 40 is added once, whatever the number of months, so it is a one-time charge. The 25, multiplied by $m$, is the monthly cost.

questions.stem: A tank is filled at a steady rate, left full for an hour, then drained quickly. Which describes the graph of water level over time?
options: Falls steadily, stays flat, then rises
Rises steeply, stays flat, then falls slowly
Rises steadily, levels off, then drops fast
questions.explanation: A steady fill is a straight rise, a full tank is a flat line, and a quick drain is a steep fall. Reversing steep and slow describes a quick fill and a slow drain.

questions.stem: A worker's shifts last week were 6, 9, 4, 8, 10 and 7 hours long. What is the median shift length?
questions.explanation: In order: 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. With six values the median is halfway between the middle two: $\frac{7 + 8}{2} = 7.5$.

questions.stem: On hotter days, a shop sells more iced drinks. A scatter plot of temperature and drinks sold would most likely show:
options: A single cluster with no pattern
questions.explanation: When one quantity rises as the other rises, the points trend up to the right, a positive association. A negative association would mean fewer drinks on hotter days.

questions.skill: Slope of a line of fit
questions.stem: A line of fit for a plant's height $y$, in centimeters, after $x$ weeks is $y = 2.5x + 4$. What does the 2.5 mean?
options: It grows about 2.5 cm each week
It is 2.5 cm tall after one week
questions.explanation: The slope is the change in height per week, about 2.5 cm. The starting height is the 4, the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.

questions.stem: A spinner landed on red 30 times in 120 spins. At that rate, about how many times would it land on red in 400 spins?
questions.explanation: Red came up $\frac{30}{120} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the time, and $\frac{1}{4} \times 400 = 100$. Adding 280 more spins to 30 is not a rate.

questions.stem: On a test, Class A had a median of 72 and a range of 30. Class B had a median of 80 and a range of 12. Which statement is supported?
options: The classes scored the same overall
Class A scored higher and more consistently
Class B scored higher and more consistently
Class B scored higher but less consistently
questions.explanation: Class B's higher median means higher typical scores, and its smaller range means scores were closer together. A larger range, like Class A's, means less consistency.

questions.stem: A wheel has a diameter of 20 inches. Using 3.14 for $\pi$, how far does it roll in one full turn?
questions.explanation: One turn covers the circumference, $C = \pi d = 3.14 \times 20 = 62.8$ inches. 125.6 uses the diameter as if it were the radius in $2\pi r$.

questions.stem: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles measures 48 degrees. What is the angle directly across from it?
questions.explanation: Vertical angles, directly across from each other, are equal, so it is 48 degrees. 132 degrees is the angle next to it, which forms a straight line with it.

questions.stem: A storage box is 4 feet long, 3 feet wide and 2 feet high. What is its volume in cubic feet?
questions.explanation: $V = lwh = 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ cubic feet. Adding the edges, $4 + 3 + 2$, gives 9, which is not a volume.

questions.stem: A triangle is slid 5 units to the right without turning or flipping it. Which is true of the new triangle?
options: It is larger than the original
It is a mirror image of the original
It is congruent to the original
questions.explanation: A slide (translation) keeps every side length and angle, so the image is congruent. A mirror image comes from a reflection, not a slide.

questions.stem: Which sentence states what the writer is asking for?
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 makes the request: keep the pool open until 8 p.m. on summer weeknights. Sentence 3 gives the problem behind it.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed because it does not support the request?
questions.explanation: A snack bar at a different pool has nothing to do with the Lincoln Street pool's hours. Sentence 5 gives a safety reason for the change.

questions.stem: Which detail would best support the request?
options: How many families swim after 5 p.m.
The temperature of the pool water
The year the pool was built
The name of the pool's head lifeguard
questions.explanation: Evidence that families already use the pool late in the day shows real demand for later hours.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to combine sentences 3 and 4?
options: The pool closes at 6 p.m., families who work during the day have no chance.
Because the pool closes at 6 p.m., working families cannot swim together.
Closing at 6 p.m., families who work during the day have no chance to swim.
The pool closes at 6 p.m. and families who work during the day.
questions.explanation: Starting with Because joins the cause and the effect in one complete sentence. Joining two sentences with only a comma is a comma splice, and the version with Closing has no clear subject for closing.

questions.skill: Transitions in a narrative of events
questions.stem: Which word or phrase would best begin sentence 3?
options: As a result of the rain,
questions.explanation: The library grew between 1912 and 1930, so a time transition connects the opening with the move. On the other hand signals a contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 3 to support it?
options: The town also has a fire station.
Some people prefer to read at home.
Hardware stores sell many kinds of tools.
By 1920, it held three thousand books.
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 says the library grew quickly, and a big rise in its books is direct evidence of that. The other sentences are off topic.

questions.stem: How is the draft organized?
questions.explanation: The draft moves from 1912 to 1930 to today, telling the library's history in time order.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Yesterday the crew ___ the new shelves before noon."

Which verb correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: Yesterday places the action in the past, so the past tense finished is correct.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The clinic changed ___ hours for the holiday."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The hours belong to the clinic, so the possessive its is correct. It's means it is.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Neither the cook nor the servers ___ the new menu yet."

Which verb correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, servers, which is plural, so have seen is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: Bring a pen, a photo ID, and your letter.
Bring a pen, a photo ID, and, your letter.
Bring, a pen, a photo ID and your letter.
Bring a pen a photo ID, and your letter.
questions.explanation: Commas separate the items in a list, with no comma after the verb or after and.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Every student must bring ___ own calculator."

Which words correctly fill the blank?
questions.explanation: Every student is singular and the blank needs a possessive, so his or her fits. Him or her is an object form, they're means they are, and their's is never correct.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The reason why the meeting was canceled is because the room was flooded."

Which revision is clearest and most concise?
options: Because of the reason that the room flooded, the meeting was canceled.
The reason the meeting was canceled is because of flooding.
The meeting was canceled because the room flooded.
The meeting, the reason being a flood, was canceled.
questions.explanation: The reason why and is because repeat the same idea. Stating the cause with because alone is clear and short.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The instructions were so ambiguous that half the class did the wrong assignment."

What does ambiguous mean?
questions.explanation: Half the class misunderstood, so the instructions could be read more than one way. Helpful instructions would not cause that.

questions.stem: The prefix pre- means "before." What does preheat mean?
questions.explanation: Pre- plus heat means to heat beforehand, as with an oven before baking. Heat again would be reheat.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The storm did a lot of bad stuff to the roof."

Which revision uses the most precise words?
options: The roof had stuff happen in the storm.
The storm tore shingles off the roof.
The storm was bad for the roof.
The storm did things to the roof.
questions.explanation: Tore shingles off says exactly what happened. Things and stuff are vague.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The study found a correlation between sleep and grades."

What does correlation mean?
questions.explanation: A correlation is a relationship in which two things tend to change together. The sentence connects sleep with grades.

questions.stem: Which word shows the strongest feeling of happiness?
questions.explanation: Pleased, content and satisfied describe mild happiness; overjoyed means extremely happy.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Sleep helps the brain save learning
Students should study through the night
questions.explanation: The passage says sleep is when much of the day's learning gets saved and supports it with two kinds of studies. It warns against all-night cramming.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that sleep helps memory of facts?
options: Cramming takes a lot of effort
Sleepers recalled more of a word list
New information is held for a short time
Some people see sleep as wasted time
questions.explanation: The word-list study compares people who slept with people who stayed awake and finds better recall after sleep. The other details set up the topic.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what would likely help a student most before a test on Friday?
options: One long study session on Thursday night
Short sessions with sleep between them
questions.explanation: The last paragraph recommends studying in shorter sessions over several days with real sleep between them. A long Thursday night session is the cramming it warns about.

questions.stem: How does the author's view of sleep differ from the view in the first sentence?
options: The author agrees sleep is wasted
The author thinks sleep is a mystery
The author says sleep hurts learning
The author sees sleep as useful work
questions.explanation: The first sentence gives the common view that sleep is wasted time; the author says researchers see it "very differently," as the time learning gets saved.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, what does "cram" mean?
options: To study hard in a short time
To review slowly over many weeks
questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts staying up all night to cram with studying over several days, so to cram is to pack study into a short time.

questions.stem: Why does Andre wait three days to open the envelope?
options: He had no time to read it
He fears it is bad news
questions.explanation: He walks past it repeatedly, and the story says thin envelopes "meant no," so he fears rejection. Passing it every day shows he had not forgotten it.

questions.stem: What news does the letter bring?
options: The college has closed for January
Kiana has been accepted to a school
Andre owes money on a bill
questions.explanation: Andre says "Classes start in January," and Kiana jumps up shouting with joy, so he has been admitted. The thin envelope turned out to be good news.

questions.stem: What does the phrase "in the voice he used for the electric bill" suggest?
options: He is excited about the letter
He thinks the letter is really a bill
He is avoiding something he dreads
questions.explanation: The electric bill is something people dread and put off, so his tone shows he is avoiding the letter. He knows it is from the college.

questions.stem: What does the narrator mean by "silence could be a kind of argument"?
options: Quiet waiting can push someone to act
Kiana was much too upset to say a word
questions.explanation: Kiana sits and waits without speaking, and her silent waiting works: Andre opens the letter. Her quiet presses him the way an argument would.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Andre smoothing the page "the way his own father used to smooth a map"?
options: To explain that his father was a driver
To show how much it matters to him
To suggest he is planning a trip
To show the letter was badly folded
questions.explanation: The gesture links him to his father and to careful handling of something important, showing what the letter means to him. It is a comparison, not a fact about a trip.

questions.stem: What is the author's main claim?
options: The bus trial should be studied more
Grand Avenue needs a bus-only lane
Drivers should pay to park on Grand
questions.explanation: The first paragraph ends with the claim, and the last paragraph repeats it: bring the bus lane back for good.

questions.stem: What reason does the author give for why bus lanes speed up trips?
options: Bus drivers can go faster than cars
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that when a bus no longer waits behind traffic, trips get faster. The author never says buses stop less.

questions.stem: How does the author respond to the shop owners' worry?
options: By noting most shoppers walk or bus
By agreeing that parking matters most
By offering shop owners free bus passes
questions.explanation: The author names the worry about parking, then answers that most shoppers arrive on foot or by bus and a faster bus brings more of them.

questions.stem: What does the table show happened to car trips during the trial?
questions.explanation: Average car trips went from 18 to 19 minutes, one minute longer. Nine minutes less is the change in bus trips (31 to 22).

questions.stem: Which detail does not support the author's argument?
options: Bus trips were shorter during the trial
The bus carries more people than the cars
Bus riders rose during the trial
questions.explanation: How often the murals are photographed has nothing to do with whether a bus lane helps riders or shops. The other details back the case for the lane.

questions.stem: According to the newspaper, why did the street flood?
options: The drains were clogged with leaves
Too much rain for the drains
questions.explanation: Officials said the drains were working but could not keep up with nearly four inches of rain in three hours. Clogged drains are the blogger's claim, not the paper's.

questions.stem: What does the resident's blog focus on most?
options: One family's night and neighbors' help
The total number of homes that flooded
The city's plan to fix the creek
questions.explanation: The blog describes the water reaching their home, the help from neighbors and the cleanup. Counts of homes and rescue boats come from the newspaper.

questions.stem: On which fact do the two accounts disagree?
options: Whether it rained on Tuesday night
questions.explanation: The newspaper reports officials saying the drains were working; the blogger does not believe that, because a drain at the corner was clogged. Both agree the street flooded after Tuesday's rain.

questions.stem: What does the newspaper account give that the blog does not?
options: How the photo albums were saved
questions.explanation: The newspaper gives street-wide facts: up to two feet of water, eleven homes evacuated, no injuries and when the street reopened. The dog and albums are personal details from the blog.
Adding two negatives moves further left on the number line: $-6 + (-9) = -15$. Getting $-3$ treats the second number as positive.

questions.stem: After a fee, a bank account balance is $-25$ dollars. A deposit of \$70 is made. What is the new balance?
questions.explanation: $-25 + 70 = 45$, so the balance is \$45. \$95 adds 25 and 70 as if the starting balance were positive.

questions.stem: Which number has the greatest absolute value?
questions.explanation: Absolute value is distance from zero: $|-9| = 9$, more than 8. 8 is the greatest number, but not the greatest distance from zero.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{9}{10}$?
questions.explanation: Multiply tops and bottoms: $\frac{18}{30} = \frac{3}{5}$. Adding them instead gives $\frac{11}{13}$.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{4}$?
questions.explanation: Use the common denominator 12: $\frac{10}{12} - \frac{3}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$. Subtracting tops and bottoms separately gives $\frac{4}{2} = 2$.

questions.stem: A car travels 150 miles on 5 gallons of gas. How many miles does it go per gallon?
questions.explanation: Miles per gallon is miles divided by gallons: $150 \div 5 = 30$.

questions.stem: A printer prints 45 pages in 3 minutes. At this rate, how many pages does it print in 8 minutes?
questions.explanation: The rate is $45 \div 3 = 15$ pages a minute, and $15 \times 8 = 120$. 135 pages is the count for 9 minutes.

questions.stem: A care home keeps a ratio of 1 nurse for every 6 residents. How many nurses are needed for 42 residents?
questions.explanation: $42 \div 6 = 7$ groups of 6, so 7 nurses.

questions.stem: Paint is mixed 2 parts blue to 5 parts white. How many quarts of blue are in 14 quarts of the mix?
questions.explanation: Each batch has $2 + 5 = 7$ parts, so 14 quarts is 2 batches of 7, with $2 \times 2 = 4$ quarts of blue. 5.6 treats blue as $\frac{2}{5}$ of the whole instead of $\frac{2}{7}$.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 60?
questions.explanation: $0.15 \times 60 = 9$. 4 comes from $60 \div 15$, which is a division, not a percent.

questions.stem: A town grew from 2,000 people to 2,500 people. By what percent did it grow?
questions.explanation: The increase is 500, and $\frac{500}{2{,}000} = 25\%$. Dividing by the new size, 2,500, gives 20%.

questions.stem: A restaurant bill is \$40, and a 20% tip is added. What is the total?
questions.explanation: 20% of 40 is 8, and $40 + 8 = 48$. \$8 is the tip alone.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $\frac{x}{4} + 3 = 8$ true?
questions.explanation: Subtract 3 to get $\frac{x}{4} = 5$, then multiply by 4: $x = 20$.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $7 - 2x = 15$ true?
questions.explanation: Subtract 7: $-2x = 8$, then divide by $-2$: $x = -4$. Dropping the negative sign gives 4.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $3(2x - 5)$?
questions.explanation: Multiply both terms by 3: $3 \cdot 2x = 6x$ and $3 \cdot 5 = 15$. $6x - 5$ forgets to multiply the 5.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $4x + 7 - x + 2$?
questions.explanation: $4x - x = 3x$ and $7 + 2 = 9$. $5x + 9$ adds the $x$ term instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: A taxi charges \$3 plus \$2 for each mile. A ride costs \$19. How many miles long was the ride?
questions.explanation: $3 + 2m = 19$, so $2m = 16$ and $m = 8$. Dividing 19 by 2 without taking off the \$3 gives 9.5.

questions.stem: A van can carry at most 1,200 pounds. The driver weighs 180 pounds, and each box weighs 40 pounds. Which inequality gives the number of boxes, $b$, the van can carry?
questions.explanation: The total weight, driver plus $40b$, can be no more than 1,200, so it is less than or equal to. The greater-than sign would mean the van must carry at least 1,200 pounds.

questions.stem: What is $\sqrt{144}$?
questions.explanation: $12 \times 12 = 144$, so $\sqrt{144} = 12$. 72 is half of 144, not its root.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped box has a volume of 64 cubic inches. How long is each edge?
questions.explanation: The edge is the cube root: $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$. 8 inches is the square root of 64, which gives the side of a square, not a cube.

questions.stem: What is $(3 \times 10^4)(2 \times 10^3)$?
questions.explanation: Multiply 3 by 2 and add the exponents: $6 \times 10^{4+3} = 6 \times 10^7$. Multiplying the exponents gives $10^{12}$.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 11)$?
questions.explanation: Slope is rise over run: $\frac{11 - 2}{4 - 1} = \frac{9}{3} = 3$.

questions.stem: Which set of ordered pairs is a function?
questions.explanation: A function gives each input exactly one output. In (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) no input repeats; in the others an input such as 4 has more than one output.

questions.stem: The graph of a proportional relationship passes through $(0, 0)$ and $(5, 30)$. What is the unit rate?
questions.explanation: The unit rate is $y$ for one unit of $x$: $30 \div 5 = 6$, which is also the slope. 30 is the value at $x = 5$, not at $x = 1$.

questions.stem: Which equation does not describe a linear function?
questions.explanation: A linear function has the form $y = mx + b$, with $x$ to the first power. $x^2$ makes a curved graph, so $y = x^2 + 1$ is not linear.

questions.stem: A food truck's daily sales were 14, 22, 9, 30 and 17 meals. What is the range?
questions.explanation: Range is greatest minus least: $30 - 9 = 21$. 17 is the median and 18.4 is the mean.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value from the mean
questions.stem: The mean of four test scores is 80. Three of the scores are 75, 82 and 90. What is the fourth score?
questions.explanation: Four scores averaging 80 total $4 \times 80 = 320$. The three known scores total 247, so the fourth is $320 - 247 = 73$.

questions.stem: The chance of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the chance it does not rain?
questions.explanation: An event and its opposite add to 1: $1 - 0.3 = 0.7$.

questions.stem: A fair number cube has faces 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling an even number greater than 2?
questions.explanation: Only 4 and 6 are even and greater than 2, so the probability is $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$. $\frac{1}{2}$ counts every even number, including 2.

questions.stem: On a scatter plot of hours studied and test scores, one student studied 1 hour and scored 98, far from all the other points. What is this point called?
questions.explanation: A point far from the pattern of the rest is an outlier. A cluster is a group of points close together.

questions.stem: A town of 20,000 people picks 5 residents at random and asks how often they exercise, then reports the result for the whole town. What is the main problem with this survey?
options: The residents were picked at random
questions.explanation: Picking at random is good, but 5 people is far too few: by chance they could all exercise a lot or hardly at all. A larger random sample gives a result much closer to the whole town's.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 50 degrees and 70 degrees. How many degrees is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees: $180 - 50 - 70 = 60$.

questions.stem: Angles $A$ and $B$ are complementary. Angle $A$ measures 34 degrees. What is the measure of angle $B$?
questions.explanation: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees: $90 - 34 = 56$. 146 uses 180, the total for supplementary angles.

questions.stem: A cube has edges 3 inches long. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: Each of the 6 faces is $3 \times 3 = 9$ square inches, and $6 \times 9 = 54$. 27 is the volume, $3^3$.

questions.stem: A triangular sail has a base of 8 feet and a height of 10 feet. What is its area?
questions.explanation: $A = \frac{1}{2}bh = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 10 = 40$. 80 forgets the one half.

questions.stem: A 6-foot person casts a 4-foot shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a 24-foot shadow. How many feet tall is the tree?
questions.explanation: The shadows make similar triangles, so height and shadow are in the same ratio: $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{24}$, and $h = 36$.

questions.stem: Two parallel lines are crossed by a third line. One angle formed measures 110 degrees. What does its corresponding angle measure?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles at parallel lines are equal, so it is 110 degrees. 70 degrees is the angle next to it on a straight line.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the writer's claim?
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 says what should happen: open until 7 p.m. two nights a week. Sentence 1 states the current hours as background.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be removed from the draft?
questions.explanation: The waiting room's paint has nothing to do with opening hours. Sentence 5 explains why patients skip checkups, which supports the claim.

questions.stem: Which word or phrase would best begin sentence 5?
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 adds another point to the survey result in sentence 4, so an addition word fits. However, In contrast and Even so all signal a contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best answer a reader who worries about the cost of evening hours?
options: Evening hours are popular in many large cities.
Many clinics keep plants in the waiting room.
The clinic is easy to find.
Staff could shift hours instead of adding them.
questions.explanation: An argument is stronger when it answers a likely objection. Shifting schedules would provide evening hours without adding staff time.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of sentence 1?
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 tells the reader why correct planting is worth the effort; the steps begin in sentence 2.

questions.stem: Which word would best begin sentence 4?
questions.explanation: Setting the tree in the hole follows removing the container, and more steps come after, so Next fits. Finally would mean it is the last step.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 6 to explain the mulch step?
options: Mulch comes in many colors and sizes.
Some trees lose their leaves in fall.
Mulch on the trunk can cause rot.
Garden centers sell mulch in bags.
questions.explanation: An explanatory text tells why a step matters, and this sentence explains why mulch is kept off the trunk. The others add facts that do not explain the step.

questions.stem: How is the draft organized?
options: As a story about one gardener
As a list of reasons for and against
As a comparison of two methods
As steps in the order they are done
questions.explanation: After its opening, the draft gives the planting steps in the order they happen, from digging to watering.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best introduce the report if it were added before sentence 1?
options: A bee colony splits its tasks three ways.
Some of the flowers in my yard are purple.
I like to put honey on my toast every day.
Bees can sting when they are scared.
questions.explanation: The report describes the queen, the workers and the drones, so an opening that names that division introduces the whole topic.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to combine sentences 2 and 3?
options: Each colony has one queen, most of the other bees are workers.
Each colony has one queen, and most other bees are workers.
Each colony has one queen and most of the other bees.
Each colony has one queen; and most other bees are workers.
questions.explanation: A comma with and correctly joins two complete sentences. A comma alone makes a comma splice, a semicolon is not followed by and, and the version ending with bees has no verb for its second part.

questions.stem: Which word in the draft is defined for the reader?
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 explains that drones are male bees with one job. The other terms are used without a definition.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best conclude the report?
options: Honey is sold in many grocery stores.
I hope to keep bees someday.
Wasps are also yellow and black.
Shared labor keeps the colony alive.
questions.explanation: A conclusion should sum up the main idea, the division of work in the colony. The other sentences drift to new topics or to the writer.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The box of tools ___ in the truck."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The subject is box, which is singular, so the verb is is. Tools is part of the phrase of tools.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Ana and ___ worked late to finish the order."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, the people who worked, so it is the subject pronoun I. Test it alone: "I worked late," not "me worked late."

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The store opens at nine the doors are locked until then."

Which revision is correct?
questions.explanation: This is a run-on: two complete sentences with nothing between them. A period after nine makes two sentences. A comma alone would be a comma splice, and the other commas are in the wrong place.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"She opened the file, read the notes and ___ the report."

Which verb correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: Opened and read are past tense, so the last verb in the series stays in the past: signed.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"The workers left ___ jackets in the break room."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: Their shows possession: the jackets belong to the workers. There is a place and they're means they are.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"We ___ finish the order until the parts arrive."

Which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: Can't is the contraction of cannot, with the apostrophe where the letters were left out.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Necessary has one c and two s's.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"Please return back the form by Friday."

Which revision removes the extra word?
options: Please return the form back to us.
Please back the form by Friday.
Please return the form by Friday.
questions.explanation: Return already means bring back, so back repeats the idea.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence.

"After the long hike, the thirsty hikers were eager to replenish their water bottles at the spring."

What does replenish mean?
questions.explanation: Thirsty hikers at a spring want more water, so replenish means to fill again.

questions.stem: The suffix -less means "without." What does careless mean?
questions.explanation: Care plus -less means without care. Full of care would be careful.

questions.stem: Which word has the most positive meaning for describing someone who saves money?
questions.explanation: Thrifty suggests wise use of money. Stingy, cheap and tight-fisted suggest being unwilling to spend or share.

questions.stem:
Read the sentences.

"The team met. The team made a plan. The team started work."

Which revision combines them most smoothly?
options: The team met, the team made a plan and worked.
Met, planned and started, the team.
The team, the plan, the work.
The team met, planned and started work.
questions.explanation: Joining the three verbs with one subject removes the repetition and keeps a complete sentence.
